analysis.one_liner: Blocks large corporations and private equity from buying up businesses during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it was introduced in June 2020, sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned large mergers and acquisitions for the duration of the COVID-19 emergency. Companies with more than $100 million in revenue, big banks, private equity funds, and registered investment advisers could not buy other firms, nor could deals involving exclusive COVID-related patents go through, unless the Federal Trade Commission unanimously granted a waiver for national security, economic, or public health reasons. Firms that broke the rule faced a blocked or reversed deal plus a penalty of at least 10% of their prior-year revenue. The ban would stay in place until the emergency ended, all states had reopened, 100 days passed, and small businesses and workers were no longer in severe financial distress.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses, independent pharmacies and medical suppliers, workers, and consumers. During a crisis when weakened companies sell cheap, the bill would have stopped $100M+ corporations, banks, and private equity funds from buying them up, which can concentrate markets, eliminate jobs, and raise prices. It also would have protected companies holding COVID-related patents from being swallowed, keeping critical production and research independent.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits acquisitions by firms with over $100 million in revenue, by banks or equity funds with over $100 million in capitalization, and by registered investment advisers during the COVID emergency [S2][S3].

Bars deals involving firms holding exclusive patents on COVID-related production, manufacturing, distribution, medical supplies, and drug development, so critical pandemic capacity could not be bought up mid-crisis [S2][S3].
Keeps the ban in place until the emergency ends, every state has reopened, 100 more days pass, and the FTC finds small businesses and workers are no longer under severe financial distress [S3].

Creates a lasting legal presumption against deals that would reduce the government's ability to produce or stockpile life-saving essential goods in a national emergency, putting the burden on the companies to prove no risk [S2][S3].
Penalizes firms attempting a prohibited deal with an order blocking or reversing it plus a fine of at least 10% of their fiscal 2019 revenue [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with over $100 million in revenue, large banks, private equity and other investment funds, and investment advisers, which would be unable to complete acquisitions until the FTC unanimously lifted the ban. Firms seeking a waiver would have to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the deal advances critical national security, economic, or public health interests. Legitimate deals that boost emergency capacity could still proceed through the waiver process, and genuinely failing firms automatically qualify for a waiver.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large firms, banks, and private equity

drawbacks.text: The moratorium is unusually broad: it covers every acquisition reportable under the Clayton Act, not just anticompetitive ones, which would freeze ordinary transactions by large firms even where no competition concerns exist [S3].

Ending the ban requires a unanimous vote of the FTC plus written agreement from several cabinet secretaries, so a single dissenting commissioner could keep the freeze going indefinitely after the crisis had passed [S3].

Some distressed-but-not-failing companies might have been better off selling to a larger firm; the bill does allow acquisitions of failing firms by deeming them to meet waiver criteria, but firms near failure that miss the strict failing-firm test would have no exit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real, documented pattern of powerful buyers picking up vulnerable companies during crises, and its core carve-outs (national security and failing-firm waivers) show the drafters tried to protect legitimate deals. The cost is that the ban sweeps in many harmless acquisitions, and the all-but-unanimous process for ending it is rigid and could outlast the emergency. On balance it was an emergency measure with a clear purpose, but its breadth would have imposed real friction on ordinary corporate transactions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in June 2020, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Pandemic Anti-Monopoly Act in the Senate on June 18, 2020, with Sen. Bernie Sanders as cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S1][S5].
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the action history shows only the introduction and referral [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and bills not passed by then expire [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations, banks, and private equity funds, which remained free to acquire weakened companies during the pandemic downturn without the restrictions the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations and private equity buyers

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no recorded floor votes or committee action; its two sponsors were a Democrat and an Independent, and no opposition was formally recorded.

industries.note: The bill barred funds with over $100 million in capitalization and registered investment advisers from any acquisitions during the emergency, cutting them off from buying companies at depressed crisis prices. Had it passed, struggling firms would have been spared private equity ownership.

Firms above the revenue threshold could not acquire any other company for the duration of the emergency, with penalties of at least 10% of prior-year revenue for violations. This would have prevented them from absorbing smaller competitors weakened by the pandemic.

industries.industry: Drug and medical supply makers with exclusive COVID-related patents
industries.note: Deals involving firms holding exclusive patents on COVID-related production, medical supplies, and drug development were prohibited outright. Keeping these firms independent protected pandemic supply chains and research capacity for the public.

The ban protected small and vulnerable firms from being bought out during the crisis, and the moratorium could not end until the FTC found small businesses and workers were no longer in severe financial distress.
